paths.title: Server & Runtime Fundamentals
paths.description: Understand trusted server execution, processes, ports, sockets, runtime lifecycle, concurrency, resources, configuration, and graceful termination.
topics: Trusted execution boundary
Backend code runs in an environment intended to enforce secrets, permissions, and authoritative business rules that clients cannot be trusted to preserve.
Place authorization, secret use, persistence rules, and invariant enforcement on the server even when the client performs matching validation.
Process model
A server process has memory, environment, open resources, signals, and a lifecycle that can end independently from individual requests.
Design startup and shutdown explicitly and avoid assuming in-memory state survives restarts or exists consistently across replicas.
Ports and sockets
Network servers listen on sockets bound to addresses and ports while clients establish connections that transport application protocols.
Bind only required interfaces, make listen ports configurable, and understand which proxy or platform actually terminates public traffic.
Runtime event sources
Network I/O, timers, filesystem operations, signals, and background work all enter the runtime through different event mechanisms.
Keep handlers bounded and avoid blocking the runtime on unnecessary synchronous CPU or I/O work.
Environment configuration
Deployments supply runtime-specific values such as database URLs, ports, feature flags, and service endpoints.
Validate required configuration at startup and fail clearly instead of discovering malformed values during live requests.
Resource lifecycle
Database connections, file descriptors, sockets, timers, and worker resources need ownership and cleanup.
Create shared resources deliberately, bound their counts, and release them during shutdown or failed initialization.
Stateless request handling
Horizontally scaled services work best when any healthy instance can process a request without hidden local session state.
Store durable or shared state in appropriate external systems and keep process-local caches explicitly disposable.
Health and readiness
Liveness indicates whether a process should be restarted while readiness indicates whether it can safely receive traffic.
Separate liveness from dependency-aware readiness and avoid expensive health checks that overload downstream services.
Signals and shutdown
Deployment platforms commonly terminate processes with signals and a grace period rather than waiting forever.
Stop accepting new work, drain in-flight requests, close resources, and exit before the platform force-kills the process.
Server observability baseline
A running process needs enough context to explain startup, shutdown, requests, failures, and resource pressure.
Emit structured startup/version/config summaries without secrets and include stable request correlation identifiers in operational telemetry.

paths.title: HTTP Semantics, Headers & Caching
paths.description: Use methods, status codes, representations, headers, conditional requests, caching, negotiation, redirects, ranges, and connection semantics correctly.
topics: Resource semantics
HTTP provides a uniform interface for acting on resources through requests and representations rather than exposing implementation details directly.
Model endpoints around clear resource or operation semantics and let method, target, headers, and content communicate intent.
Method semantics
GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, and other methods have different safety, idempotency, and cache expectations.
Choose methods from protocol semantics and implement retries only when the operation's actual behavior tolerates repetition.
Status code families
2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx codes communicate broad outcome classes while specific codes help clients choose behavior.
Return the most specific stable status your contract supports and do not encode every outcome as 200 with a custom error flag.
Representation metadata
Content-Type describes the media type of a representation while Content-Encoding and language metadata describe additional interpretation.
Send accurate metadata and reject unsupported request media types rather than guessing how to parse ambiguous bodies.
Content negotiation
Accept-family headers let clients express representation preferences that servers may satisfy or decline.
Negotiate only dimensions your API intentionally supports and include Vary when caches must distinguish responses by request headers.
Conditional requests
ETag and Last-Modified validators allow clients to revalidate cached representations or protect updates against lost writes.
Use If-None-Match for efficient cache validation and If-Match or equivalent version checks when concurrent update safety matters.
Cache-Control
Freshness, revalidation, shared/private storage, and no-store directives determine how HTTP caches may reuse responses.
Define cache policy per representation and avoid caching personalized or sensitive responses in shared caches accidentally.
Redirect semantics
301, 302, 303, 307, and 308 differ in permanence and method-preservation behavior.
Choose redirects deliberately and avoid redirect chains or open redirect targets derived from untrusted input.
Header trust boundaries
Forwarded, Host, Origin, Authorization, cookies, and proxy-added headers have security meaning only when the deployment trust chain is understood.
Configure trusted proxies explicitly and never trust spoofable forwarding headers from arbitrary clients.
Request limits and timeouts
HTTP servers need limits for headers, body sizes, idle connections, and processing time to preserve resources.
Set bounded limits appropriate to the endpoint and return clear failure behavior instead of allowing unbounded resource consumption.
codeExamples:
GET /articles/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json
If-None-Match: "v7"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "v7"

paths.title: API Design, Contracts & Evolution
paths.description: Design REST, RPC, GraphQL, schemas, pagination, errors, versioning, compatibility, idempotency, and discoverable contracts around real client needs.
topics: Contract-first thinking
An API contract defines inputs, outputs, errors, semantics, and compatibility expectations independently from handler implementation.
Write representative requests, responses, error cases, and invariants before coding endpoints that multiple clients will depend on.
REST resource modeling
REST-style APIs represent resources and use standard HTTP semantics to manipulate or retrieve their representations.
Use stable nouns, relationships, and method semantics instead of encoding every action into ad hoc verb-heavy URLs.
RPC modeling
RPC APIs expose named operations and structured arguments, which can be clearer for command-oriented domain behavior.
Use RPC when the core contract is an operation rather than pretending a complex command is ordinary CRUD.
GraphQL modeling
GraphQL lets clients select fields from a typed schema but shifts complexity into resolvers, cost control, authorization, and caching.
Authorize at domain/object boundaries, limit query cost, and avoid exposing internal data models merely because the schema can represent them.
Schema definitions
Machine-readable schemas document required fields, formats, enums, nullability, and nested structures.
Keep schemas executable in validation or contract tests so documentation and runtime behavior cannot drift silently.
Pagination
Large collections require bounded page sizes and a stable continuation strategy under concurrent inserts or deletes.
Prefer cursor-based pagination for frequently changing ordered datasets and document ordering plus continuation semantics explicitly.
Filtering and sorting
Flexible query parameters can accidentally expose expensive or unauthorized query capabilities.
Allowlist supported filters and sort fields, validate ranges, and align database indexes with high-value query patterns.
Error contract
Clients need stable machine-readable error codes plus human-readable context without internal stack traces or secrets.
Return a consistent error envelope with correlation metadata and preserve field-level validation details where useful.
Versioning and compatibility
Breaking changes require a migration strategy because deployed clients rarely upgrade simultaneously.
Prefer additive compatible evolution, deprecate with telemetry and timelines, and version only when a genuine contract break cannot be avoided.
Idempotency keys
Some non-idempotent operations such as payments or provisioning need a way to distinguish retries from new intent.
Persist idempotency keys with request identity and outcome so repeated equivalent submissions return the original result safely.
codeExamples: {"error":{"code":"validation_failed","message":"Request is invalid","fields":{"email":"Must be a valid email address"},"requestId":"req_123"}}

paths:

    get:
      parameters:
        - in: query
          name: cursor

      responses:
        '200':

paths.title: Node.js Async Runtime & Concurrency
paths.description: Understand the event loop, promises, streams, worker threads, process errors, timers, cancellation, backpressure, and CPU versus I/O concurrency.
topics: Event loop
Node coordinates callbacks and asynchronous I/O through an event loop, so long synchronous work delays unrelated requests.
Keep request-path CPU work bounded and measure event-loop delay when responsiveness degrades under load.
Promises and async functions
Promise continuations express asynchronous completion but do not make CPU-heavy JavaScript execute in parallel automatically.
Use async/await for I/O orchestration and move genuinely CPU-intensive work to worker threads or external workers.
Microtasks
Promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks run at specific scheduling points and can starve other work when recursively overused.
Avoid unbounded microtask chains and understand scheduling when debugging ordering or starvation defects.
Timers
setTimeout and setInterval provide minimum-delay scheduling rather than real-time guarantees.
Use timers for approximate scheduling only and put durable scheduled jobs in a system that survives process restarts.
Streams
Readable, Writable, Duplex, and Transform streams process data incrementally and expose backpressure.
Stream large files or bodies instead of buffering everything in memory, and use pipeline helpers to propagate errors and cleanup.
Backpressure
When a producer outpaces a consumer, unchecked buffering increases memory and latency until the process becomes unstable.
Respect write return values or use pipeline/stream abstractions that coordinate flow automatically.
Worker threads
Worker threads run JavaScript in parallel within one process and communicate through messages or shared memory.
Use workers for expensive CPU tasks with measurable benefit and bound the worker pool instead of creating one thread per request.
AbortSignal
AbortController provides a standard cancellation signal for fetch and many Node APIs.
Propagate one request-scoped signal through downstream calls so abandoned or timed-out work can stop consuming resources.
Unhandled failures
Uncaught exceptions and unhandled promise rejections indicate lost failure boundaries and may leave process state unreliable.
Log enough context, terminate when process integrity is uncertain, and rely on a supervisor to restart rather than continuing blindly.
Runtime diagnostics
CPU profiles, heap snapshots, diagnostic reports, event-loop metrics, and async stack traces reveal runtime bottlenecks and leaks.
Capture diagnostics around reproducible symptoms before changing concurrency settings by guesswork.

paths.title: Routing, Middleware & Handler Architecture
paths.description: Organize route matching, middleware, request context, controllers, domain services, dependency boundaries, and response ownership without creating hidden control flow.
topics: Route matching
A route combines method, path pattern, and sometimes host or content constraints to select behavior.
Keep route patterns predictable and reject ambiguous overlaps that make ownership depend on registration order.
Middleware purpose
Middleware handles cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, logging, parsing, rate limits, and headers around route execution.
Keep middleware focused, ordered deliberately, and explicit about whether it terminates the request or calls the next stage.
Request context
A request-scoped context can carry identity, correlation IDs, deadlines, locale, and validated metadata through layers.
Create context once at the edge and pass only trusted normalized values rather than repeatedly reparsing raw headers.
Thin handlers
Route handlers become maintainable when HTTP translation is separated from reusable domain behavior.
Parse and validate at the handler boundary, call domain services, then translate typed outcomes into HTTP responses.
Domain services
Business rules should not depend directly on framework request/response objects when they must be reused or tested independently.
Pass domain values and explicit dependencies into services instead of importing global framework state.
Dependency injection
Explicit dependencies make external services replaceable in tests and clarify what code needs to operate.
Inject repositories, clocks, queues, and clients through constructors or factories rather than hiding them behind mutable globals.
Error propagation
Frameworks differ in how thrown or rejected failures reach centralized error handling.
Define one error boundary that converts known domain errors predictably and reports unknown failures without leaking internals.
Response ownership
Multiple layers writing headers or bodies can produce duplicate sends, partial responses, or inconsistent status codes.
Assign one clear layer responsibility for final HTTP response construction and make early middleware termination explicit.
Route-level policy
Authentication, authorization, body limits, cache rules, and rate limits may vary significantly by route.
Declare policy close to route registration so security behavior is reviewable rather than hidden across distant middleware.
Modular routing
Large backends need route ownership aligned with feature or domain boundaries rather than one global file.
Group routes with their handlers, schemas, services, and tests while preserving shared infrastructure as narrow platform modules.
